newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghans fleeing Taleban seek refuge in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Afghans fleeing Taleban seek refuge in Pakistan.

text.p: At least 10,000 Afghans have fled to Pakistan since the capture of Kabul by the radical Islamic Taleban militia, a U.N. official said on Monday.

"About 9,000 to 10,000 people have come to the Nasir Bagh camp on the outskirts of Peshawar," Anoush Daneshwar, deputy head of mission for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) told Reuters in Islamabad.
"The real figure (of arrivals in Pakistan) is much higher because many people go and stay with their relatives and are not registered by UNHCR or the Pakistani authorities," he said.

Daneshwar said 50 to 70 families a day had been heading east from Kabul in the past week, but described this as fairly normal traffic for the time of year, when many people move to the eastern city of Jalalabad to escape the harsh Kabul winter.

The Taleban, who swept triumphantly into the Afghan capital on September 27, immediately began imposing their strict version of Islamic Sharia law, telling women to stay at home and men to grow beards and pray five times daily at mosques.

Many educated Kabulis decided that life under the Taleban would be intolerable and made plans to leave, but Taleban fighters intervened at crowded bus stations to stop men from taking families or household goods with them, witnesses said.
But Daneshwar, just back from a trip to Kabul, said there was no panic among ordinary people, who have in the past fled from heavy bouts of fighting in Afghanistan's long civil war.
"The population is basically sitting tight," he said. "Food is available and security is satisfactory for most people."

The conflict, however, has swirled closer to Kabul in the past two days as guerrillas loyal to ousted government commander Ahmad Shah Masood drive the Taleban out of territory to the north which the Islamic warriors had captured earlier.
At the Nasir Bagh refugee camp in Peshawar, the new arrivals, mostly from Jalalabad, are confined to a mud-walled enclosure behind a large steel gate, witnesses said.
Muhammad Younas Khan, district administrator for Pakistan's Commissionerate for Afghan Refugees, said the authorities were encouraging newcomers to return home as soon as possible.
He said seven or eight families of urban Afghans were crossing into Pakistan every day, but went straight to the homes of their relatives already here, rather than to the camp.
Pakistan hosted about three million Afghan refugees during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s and more than a million have yet to return to their shattered country.
The refugees in Nasir Bagh, lacking radios or electricity, have little idea of what is going on in Afghanistan and crowd around visitors to the camp for the latest news.
In the established part of the camp, Afghan girls aged six to 18 gather in primitive tented schools run by aid agencies.
Talah (Eds: one name), a young Afghan woman school teacher, said the Taleban ban on women working was unfair, especially to the thousands of war widows now unable to feed their families.
"The Taleban should make rules for women flexible so that both men and women can play their due role in reconstructing our war-devastated country," she said, adjusting her headscarf.
